target: AG1’s claim that a national Election Day holiday would remove scheduling barriers for many Americans
objection: A federal holiday would not reliably remove the biggest voting barrier for low-income workers, because federal law does not require private employers to give paid holiday time off and retail/service workers would often still have to work or lose wages to vote.

target: AG1’s assumption that a holiday would reliably help low-income workers more than it harms them
objection: Low-income workers may actually be worse off under a federal Election Day holiday because they are the least able to absorb unpaid time or lost wages, so the policy can increase their opportunity costs instead of reducing them.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday would meaningfully increase turnout by reducing scheduling barriers
objection: Research was cited to argue that an election-day holiday by itself is not an effective way to raise turnout, especially compared with other voting-access reforms, so the turnout benefit is not reliable or substantial on its own.

target: AG1’s suggestion that a holiday would reduce the practical burdens low-income workers face when voting
objection: A holiday can reduce work/school conflicts but still leave other major time costs untouched, and because polling places, transportation, and voter-assistance services may operate with reduced hours on holidays, voting may become less accessible rather than easier.

target: AG2’s claim that a reform must reliably give workers paid or protected time off to matter
objection: That standard is too narrow because turnout is influenced by more than whether workers get guaranteed paid time off; making voting feel like a civic celebration can increase motivation and turnout even if some opportunity costs remain.

target: AG2’s claim that a federal holiday would mostly fail to help low-income workers because employers are not required to give paid holiday leave
objection: Even without a legal mandate, many private workplaces and public institutions close or reduce hours on federal holidays, so a national Election Day holiday would still give many low-income workers more daytime availability and lower opportunity costs.

target: AG2’s claim that other reforms are better because they more directly address time barriers
objection: The broader point is that school and work schedules already prevent millions of Americans from voting, and moving Election Day to a holiday directly targets those scheduling constraints in a way that makes voting more feasible for more people.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday would generally solve low-income workers’ scheduling barriers
objection: Many low-income workers are in retail, service, or other essential jobs that continue on holidays, so a federal holiday would not reliably translate into paid or protected time for the people most burdened by voting opportunity costs.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday reduces low-income workers’ opportunity costs
objection: If low-income workers still must work or absorb unpaid time on Election Day, the policy fails to reliably reduce their costs and may even make them worse off, so it is a distributionally risky strategy compared with enforceable alternatives.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday would reliably translate into more available time for low-income workers
objection: Voting on Election Day also takes time for travel, waiting, and completing the ballot, so the core cost is not just missing work; a day off does not eliminate those time burdens.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday would lower low-income voters’ opportunity costs overall
objection: When more people are free to vote at the same time, polling places can become more crowded and wait times can rise, which can offset or even outweigh the scheduling benefit of the holiday for low-income voters who have less flexibility to absorb extra time costs.

target: AG2’s claim that in-person voting time costs undermine the holiday proposal
objection: The main burden for low-income voters is often the conflict between voting and daytime work or school, so if a holiday removes that conflict, the same travel and waiting time becomes less costly overall than it would be on a normal workday.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday would not reliably reduce opportunity costs for low-income voters
objection: A holiday also eases related household, childcare, transportation, and caregiving disruptions that are tied to ordinary work/school routines, so it can reduce more than just wage loss and still lower overall opportunity costs for low-income voters.

target: AG1’s assumption that holiday scheduling would not significantly worsen voting access
objection: Polling-place capacity is limited, and a holiday could shift more people into same-day in-person voting while some workers or facilities become less available, which would raise wait times and create new access problems rather than simply removing barriers.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday would make voting more feasible without major downsides
objection: Because a holiday can both increase demand at polling places and reduce the availability of election workers or host facilities, it can systematically worsen polling access and make voting less reliable on Election Day.
